# Linking and equating {#linking}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* explain why two separately calibrated forms are not on the same scale;
* describe common-item (anchor) and common-person designs;
* link two calibrations with the mean-sigma and Stocking-Lord methods;
* check anchor items for parameter drift;
* run a concurrent calibration with a multiple-group model;
* carry a cut score from one form to another with IRT true-score equating.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[linking](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#linking),
[anchor items](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#anchor-items),
[moment linking](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#moment-linking),
[characteristic curve linking](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#characteristic-curve-linking),
[parameter drift](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#parameter-drift),
[test characteristic curve](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#test-characteristic-curve).

## The ideas

Every calibration fixes the scale by assuming that the people in it have
$\theta$ with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. If this year's candidates are
stronger than last year's, a separate calibration of this year's form will
still put *them* at mean 0, and every item will look harder than it is. To
compare forms, or groups, the two calibrations must be put on a common
scale. That is **linking**; when the goal is to make scores on two forms
interchangeable, it is called **equating** [@kolen2014].

Because the IRT scale is only determined up to a linear transformation,
linking amounts to finding two constants $A$ and $B$ such that, for the new
form's parameters,

$$\theta^* = A\theta + B, \qquad b^* = A b + B, \qquad a^* = a / A.$$

The constants come from information the two calibrations share. In the
common design, the **non-equivalent groups with anchor test** (NEAT) design,
the two forms share a set of **anchor items**. Two families of methods
estimate $A$ and $B$ from the anchors.

* **Moment methods.** *Mean-sigma* matches the mean and standard deviation of
  the anchor difficulties: $A = s_{b,\text{old}} / s_{b,\text{new}}$ and
  $B = \bar b_\text{old} - A\,\bar b_\text{new}$. They are simple, but
  sensitive to a single unusual anchor.
* **Characteristic curve methods.** *Stocking-Lord* [@stocking1983] chooses
  $A$ and $B$ to make the anchors' test characteristic curve (the expected
  anchor score as a function of $\theta$) as similar as possible on the two
  scales. They use all the parameters at once and are more robust.

An alternative to linking two separate calibrations is **concurrent
calibration**: Fit one multiple-group model to both forms, constraining the
anchor items to be equal across groups and estimating the new group's mean
and standard deviation.

Everything rests on the anchors behaving the same way in both
administrations. An anchor whose parameters have changed, because it was
exposed, taught to, or its position or wording changed, shows **parameter
drift**, and it must be removed from the anchor set before linking.

## Example 1: Separate calibration and linking

A language school has an old and a new 30-item placement test that share 10
anchor items. We simulate 1,000 students on each. The new cohort is stronger
(mean 0.4, standard deviation 1.1), and anchor A06 was leaked and became
easier on the new form.

```{r data-linking-1}
# Simulated NEAT design: old form (O01-O20 + anchors A01-A10) and new form
# (N01-N20 + the same anchors); anchor A06 drifts on the new form.
set.seed(1010)
anchors <- sprintf("A%02d", 1:10)
pars <- data.frame(item = c(sprintf("O%02d", 1:20), sprintf("N%02d", 1:20), anchors),
                   a = rlnorm(50, 0.15, 0.25), b = rnorm(50, 0, 1))
gen <- function(items, n, mean, sd, shift = NULL) {
  p <- pars[match(items, pars$item), ]
  if (!is.null(shift)) p$b[p$item %in% names(shift)] <- p$b[p$item %in% names(shift)] + shift
  out <- simdata(matrix(p$a), matrix(-p$a * p$b), N = n, itemtype = "2PL",
                 Theta = matrix(rnorm(n, mean, sd)))
  colnames(out) <- items
  as.data.frame(out)
}
old <- gen(c(sprintf("O%02d", 1:20), anchors), 1000, 0, 1)
new <- gen(c(sprintf("N%02d", 1:20), anchors), 1000, 0.4, 1.1, shift = c(A06 = -1.2))
```

Calibrate each form on its own:

```{r}
fit_old <- mirt(old, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
fit_new <- mirt(new, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
p_old <- coef(fit_old, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[anchors, c("a", "b")]
p_new <- coef(fit_new, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[anchors, c("a", "b")]
round(cbind(b_old = p_old[, "b"], b_new = p_new[, "b"]), 2)
```

The anchors look easier on the new calibration, because the new students are
stronger and their calibration puts them at mean 0. Before linking, check
for drift. On a common scale the anchor difficulties should lie on a straight
line:

```{r anchor-drift, fig.height = 3.6, fig.width = 4.5, out.width = "60%", fig.cap = "Anchor difficulties in the old and new calibrations; items off the line may have drifted."}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data.frame(old = p_old[, "b"], new = p_new[, "b"], item = anchors),
       aes(new, old)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey70", formula = y ~ x) +
  geom_point() + geom_text(aes(label = item), nudge_y = 0.15, size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Difficulty, new calibration", y = "Difficulty, old calibration") +
  theme_mirtverse()
```

A06 sits well off the line formed by the others. A simple rule is to flag
anchors whose difference in difficulty is far from the typical difference:

```{r}
diff_b <- p_old[, "b"] - p_new[, "b"]
round(sort((diff_b - median(diff_b)) / mad(diff_b)), 1)
```

We drop A06 from the anchor set and compute the mean-sigma constants from the
remaining nine:

```{r}
keep <- setdiff(anchors, "A06")
A <- sd(p_old[keep, "b"]) / sd(p_new[keep, "b"])
B <- mean(p_old[keep, "b"]) - A * mean(p_new[keep, "b"])
c(A = A, B = B)
```

$B$ estimates how much stronger the new cohort is on the old scale (we
simulated 0.4), and $A$ how much more spread out (1.1). Stocking-Lord finds
the constants that make the two anchor characteristic curves agree:

```{r}
tcc <- function(a, b, theta) sapply(theta, function(t) sum(plogis(a * (t - b))))
grid <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 41)
sl_loss <- function(k) {
  A <- k[1]; B <- k[2]
  sum((tcc(p_old[keep, "a"], p_old[keep, "b"], grid) -
       tcc(p_new[keep, "a"] / A, A * p_new[keep, "b"] + B, grid))^2 * dnorm(grid))
}
sl <- optim(c(1, 0), sl_loss)$par
c(A = sl[1], B = sl[2])
```

Both methods recover the cohort difference well. What would have happened
if we had kept the drifted anchor?

```{r}
A_all <- sd(p_old[, "b"]) / sd(p_new[, "b"])
c(A = A_all, B = mean(p_old[, "b"]) - A_all * mean(p_new[, "b"]))
```

One leaked item is enough to distort the link, and with it every score on
the new form.

## Example 2: Concurrent calibration and equating a pass mark

Concurrent calibration fits both forms at once. We stack the two datasets;
each student has `NA` for the items they did not take.

```{r data-linking-2}
# The same NEAT data stacked: NA for items not on a student's form.
# A06 is renamed on the new form, so it is not treated as an anchor.
new_a <- new; names(new_a)[names(new_a) == "A06"] <- "A06_new"
resp <- merge(transform(old, form = "old", id = seq_len(nrow(old))),
              transform(new_a, form = "new", id = nrow(old) + seq_len(nrow(new_a))),
              all = TRUE)
form <- factor(resp$form, levels = c("old", "new"))
resp <- resp[, setdiff(names(resp), c("form", "id"))]
```

Renaming A06 on the new form turns it into two separate items, one per form,
which is the usual way to drop a drifted anchor from the link without
discarding its responses. `multipleGroup()` constrains every item to have the
same parameters in both groups (each unique item is only seen by one group
anyway) and frees the new group's mean and variance:

```{r}
mg <- suppressWarnings(
  multipleGroup(resp, 1, group = form, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE,
                invariance = c(colnames(resp), "free_means", "free_var")))
coef(mg, simplify = TRUE)$new[c("means", "cov")]
```

The new group's mean and variance are estimated on the old group's scale, and
are close to the values we simulated (0.4 and $1.1^2 = 1.21$).

Now the pass mark. The old form's pass mark was 18 correct out of 30. What
score on the new form corresponds to the same ability? **IRT true-score
equating** finds the $\theta$ at which the old form's expected score (its test
characteristic curve) equals 18, then reads off the new form's expected score
at that $\theta$.

```{r}
items <- coef(mg, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$old$items
old_items <- c(sprintf("O%02d", 1:20), anchors)
new_items <- c(sprintf("N%02d", 1:20), setdiff(anchors, "A06"), "A06_new")
tcc_form <- function(ids, theta) tcc(items[ids, "a"], items[ids, "b"], theta)
theta_cut <- uniroot(function(t) tcc_form(old_items, t) - 18, c(-4, 4))$root
c(theta_cut = theta_cut, new_form_cut = tcc_form(new_items, theta_cut))
```

```{r tcc-forms, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Test characteristic curves of the old and new forms on the common scale, with the cut score."}
curves <- data.frame(theta = rep(grid, 2),
                     score = c(tcc_form(old_items, grid), tcc_form(new_items, grid)),
                     form = rep(c("Old form", "New form"), each = length(grid)))
ggplot(curves, aes(theta, score, colour = form)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = theta_cut, linetype = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 18, linetype = 3) +
  labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Expected number correct", colour = NULL) +
  theme_mirtverse()
```

If the new form is easier, its curve lies above the old form's and the pass
mark on the new form is higher; if it is harder, the pass mark is lower.
Here the new form is a little easier, so the old pass mark of 18 corresponds
to about `r round(tcc_form(new_items, theta_cut), 1)` on the new form.
Rounding the equated score to a whole number is a policy decision: Rounding
down passes slightly more candidates than the old standard, rounding up
slightly fewer.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Repeat the mean-sigma link in Example 1 with the *mean-mean* method:
   $A = \bar a_\text{new} / \bar a_\text{old}$, $B = \bar b_\text{old} - A\,\bar
   b_\text{new}$. How close are the constants to the Stocking-Lord ones?
2. Rerun the concurrent calibration of Example 2 *with* A06 as an anchor.
   How much does the estimated mean of the new group change?
3. Compute the pass mark on the new form if the old pass mark were 22.
4. A board member asks why the pass mark changed from one year to the next
   "when the standard was supposed to stay the same". Answer in two sentences.
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
A_mm <- mean(p_new[keep, "a"]) / mean(p_old[keep, "a"])
c(A = A_mm, B = mean(p_old[keep, "b"]) - A_mm * mean(p_new[keep, "b"]))

resp_all <- merge(transform(old, form = "old", id = seq_len(nrow(old))),
                  transform(new, form = "new", id = nrow(old) + seq_len(nrow(new))),
                  all = TRUE)
form_all <- factor(resp_all$form, levels = c("old", "new"))
resp_all <- resp_all[, setdiff(names(resp_all), c("form", "id"))]
mg_all <- suppressWarnings(
  multipleGroup(resp_all, 1, group = form_all, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE,
                invariance = c(colnames(resp_all), "free_means", "free_var")))
coef(mg_all, simplify = TRUE)$new$means

theta22 <- uniroot(function(t) tcc_form(old_items, t) - 22, c(-4, 4))$root
tcc_form(new_items, theta22)
```

2. With A06 treated as an anchor, the new group's mean rises well above the
   simulated 0.4. The model has to explain why the new students do so much
   better on A06; since A06 is constrained to be the same item, part of the
   leak is credited to the students' ability. Every new-form score would be
   too high.
4. For example: "The standard is the same level of ability, not the same
   number of questions. This year's form was a little easier, so reaching
   that level of ability takes a slightly higher number of correct answers."

</details>

## Further reading {-}

Kolen and Brennan [-@kolen2014] is the standard reference on equating and
linking. Stocking and Lord [-@stocking1983] introduced the characteristic
curve method used here.
